items.prompt: In the opening scenario, how many of the 4 contributions did the manager recall unaided?
choices: One
Three
All four
items.explanation: Only the flashy demo was recalled; the other three were forgotten.

items.prompt: What does memory favor most?
choices: Quiet, competent routine work
Work done long ago on weekends
Recent and dramatic events
items.explanation: Memory keeps what is recent, dramatic, or witnessed.

items.prompt: A brag doc is best described as:
choices: A yearly letter that a manager writes alone
A personal running log of work and its impact
A complaint filed with HR to demand a promotion decision
items.explanation: It is the engineer's own ongoing record, not a one-off manager document.

items.prompt: When should a brag doc entry be written?
choices: Soon after the work happens
Only on the night before the review
Never, because good work is self-evident
items.explanation: Detail fades fast, so entries are made close to the event.

items.prompt: Visibility means:
choices: How good the work itself actually was
How many coworkers sit near your desk each day
How well decision-makers know what you did
items.explanation: Visibility is about awareness among the people who decide, not about quality.

items.prompt: Which contribution did the manager remember?
choices: The Saturday production bug fix
The demo from two months ago
The mentoring conversations over the half-year
items.explanation: The demo was recent and visible, which is why it survived.

items.prompt: What replaces the manager's memory as the record?
choices: The brag doc
A longer meeting
Hoping for the best
items.explanation: The log is the record, so memory no longer has to be.

items.prompt: What is wrong with 'the work should speak for itself'?
choices: It wrongly claims that good work matters at all
It only ever applies to weekend side projects
It assumes someone listens and remembers for months
items.explanation: Almost nothing meets the standard of constant, lasting attention.

items.prompt: Two engineers did equally good work. One kept a log; the other relied on the manager. At review time the manager has the same busy six months behind them. Which prediction fits the unit?
choices: Both packets match, since a manager who values the work will remember all of it
The other packet is richer, since relying on the manager's attention forces closer observation
The logger's packet is weaker, since written entries make a manager trust the work less than before
The logger's packet holds more of the real work, since the record stands apart from recall
items.explanation: The log removes the dependence on recall; good work alone does not guarantee a packet.
items.reference:
Memory vs. record
🧠 memory keeps recent, dramatic, witnessed work
📓 a brag doc keeps what was written the week it happened
👁️ visibility is separate from quality
Why: unaided memory is a poor archive, so the record must not depend on it.
items.learnMore:
Quiet work is forgotten first

Nobody is at fault. Memory favors the vivid and the recent, so quiet competent work needs a written trace made close to when it happened.

Common mistake

Assuming good work will be noticed on its own. Quality and visibility are two separate things.
items.reflection: Think of a contribution of yours from the last six months that a colleague would probably not remember. What trace of it exists today?

items.prompt: The bug fix was real, valuable, and forgotten. What does the opening scenario show about that outcome?
choices: The manager was careless, since any competent manager would have kept every detail
The work was less valuable, since important work is always remembered by managers
Quality and visibility can diverge, so strong work can still leave a thin packet
The engineer should have shouted about it on the day, to force the manager's attention
items.explanation: Nothing about the manager's character is needed to explain it; memory simply keeps the vivid.

items.prompt: Which is objective framing?
choices: I did a great job on the whole migration
Query latency fell from 400ms to 60ms (example)
I was a true asset to the entire team
items.explanation: It states a before-and-after fact a reader can check.

items.prompt: 'I did a great job' is:
choices: A self-assessment
A measurable fact
A before-and-after number
items.explanation: It is a verdict about the writer's own quality.

items.prompt: What does a verdict ask the reader to do?
choices: Check a fact on their own
Compare two numbers side by side
Take the writer's word
items.explanation: A verdict asks for agreement without giving evidence.

items.prompt: What does a fact give the reader?
choices: A request for praise
Something to evaluate
A reason to skim past it
items.explanation: Facts can be judged independently.

items.prompt: Subjective means:
choices: 'Believe me, I was good'
'This happened, and this changed'
'See the attached chart'
items.explanation: Subjective statements rest on the writer's opinion.

items.prompt: Objective means:
choices: 'Trust me, I was good at it'
'I feel very proud of this one'
'This happened, and this changed'
items.explanation: Objective statements describe events and effects.

items.prompt: Why does objective framing feel less like bragging?
choices: It simply uses a lot more adjectives
The writer reports instead of grading
It hides what actually happened
items.explanation: The verdict is left to the reader.

items.prompt: Which sentence is a verdict?
choices: I was a huge asset to the project
Cut the maintenance window to forty minutes (example)
Fixed 12 records by hand (example)
items.explanation: 'Huge asset' is a judgment of the writer.

items.prompt: A writer replaces 'I led the migration brilliantly' with 'I led the migration very effectively.' Has the problem been fixed?
choices: Yes, since 'effectively' is a plainer, less boastful word than 'brilliantly'
No, both are verdicts about the writer; a before-and-after fact is still missing
Yes, since removing the adjective that sounds like praise removes the self-assessment
No, since the sentence needed more adjectives to make its point clearly enough
items.explanation: Softer wording changes tone but not the kind of claim; only checkable facts do.
items.reference:
Verdict vs. fact
🗣️ subjective: 'I did a great job' asks for agreement
📏 objective: 'latency fell from 400ms to 60ms' (example) can be checked
the reader draws the conclusion
Why: a fact invites evaluation; a verdict invites you to take the writer's word.
items.learnMore:
Why facts feel safer

The discomfort of self-promotion tracks the verdict, not the facts. Reporting what happened and what changed lets the reader grade the work, not the writer.

Common mistake

Believing that softer wording fixes the problem. Hedged praise is still a verdict.
items.reflection: Pick something you are proud of. Can you restate it as a fact someone could check, with no adjective about yourself?

items.prompt: Why is 'cut latency from 400ms to 60ms' (example) not a disguised boast?
choices: It states a fact the reader can judge, so the writer is not grading themselves
It is a number, and numbers are never read as self-promotion by any audience
It is shorter, and short sentences cannot carry any opinion about the writer
It names the team, and sharing credit is what makes a claim count as objective
items.explanation: The claim itself differs: a checkable fact versus a request to trust the writer.

Check it against facts, since the sentence already lists what the writer did
Ignore the writer, since a person's own notes are never worth reading at all
Little, because it offers no evidence to weigh, only a conclusion to accept
items.explanation: A verdict with no facts leaves the reader nothing to evaluate.

choices: It is modest on purpose, since leaving out impact shows good character
It is dishonest, since only the writer's own verdict can capture the real value
It is not modest at all; it names the full impact in checkable terms
It is neutral, since facts and verdicts carry the same amount of information

items.prompt: How many parts does a usable entry need?
choices: Three
One
Seven
items.explanation: What changed, why it mattered, and what was hard.

items.prompt: 'What changed' means:
choices: The writer's own current job title
The date of the next review
The concrete before and after
items.explanation: It is the difference the work made.

items.prompt: 'Why it mattered' covers:
choices: The color scheme of the document
The stakes: who was affected
The first name of the manager
items.explanation: It states what the work prevented or unblocked.

items.prompt: 'What was hard' points to:
choices: The judgment call or ambiguity
The length of the commute
The font used in the entry
items.explanation: It marks why the work was worth recording.

items.prompt: Which is a topic, not an entry?
choices: Cut deploy time from 20 to 8 minutes (example)
Owned the cutover step and shortened downtime (example)
Improved the deploy pipeline
items.explanation: It names the area without any of the three parts.

items.prompt: A judgment call is:
choices: A phone call to a manager
A decision with no obvious answer
A routine, scripted task
items.explanation: The person had to choose with care.

items.prompt: Should an entry include a number?
choices: Yes, when a real one exists
Always, even an invented one
Never, under any circumstances
items.explanation: Use real numbers; never fabricate.

items.prompt: Which work usually deserves an entry?
choices: Every routine click
Only work that took exactly a weekend
Work involving judgment calls
items.explanation: Routine work rarely needs one; judgment work usually does.

items.prompt: Entry: 'Reduced incident count from 9 to 3 in a quarter (example); the on-call team no longer gets paged overnight.' Which part is missing?
choices: What changed, since no before-and-after figure appears in the sentence
What was hard, since nothing shows the judgment or ambiguity involved in the work
Why it mattered, since the stakes for the people affected are not mentioned
Nothing is missing, since a number and a result make an entry complete
items.explanation: It has a before and after and the overnight stakes; the hard part is absent.
items.reference:
Three parts of an entry
🔁 what changed: before and after
⚠️ why it mattered: who, what it prevented
🧩 what was hard: the judgment call
Why: each part answers a question the writer will have forgotten in six months.
items.learnMore:
A topic is not an entry

'Improved the pipeline' names a subject. A useful entry also carries the change, the stakes, and the hard part, because memory will not.

Common mistake

Writing a title and calling it a record. Six months on, the title explains nothing.
items.reflection: Take one line from your current notes. Which of the three parts does it lack?

items.prompt: Two entries describe the same fix. One adds only 'it was a really big deal.' What does that addition give a future reader?
choices: Nothing checkable; it is a verdict where stakes or difficulty should be
The stakes, since calling something big is a way of describing why it mattered
The hard part, since size is the same thing as difficulty in practice
The before and after, since 'big' implies something changed by a lot
items.explanation: None of the three parts is a size adjective; each is a concrete fact.

items.prompt: Six months later, which missing part most limits a manager's use of an entry about a cross-team dependency?
choices: The date, since an entry without a date cannot be linked to any real event
The team name, since the entry needs a label before a manager can read it
The tool used, since managers weigh the work by the software involved
What was hard, because the sequencing is the evidence of judgment
items.explanation: Coordination is the non-routine part; if it is unrecorded, it is invisible.

items.prompt: A writer has a real before-and-after number but no stakes. What is the best next addition?
choices: A second number, since two figures prove more than one fact does in a log
A sentence of praise, since stakes are best conveyed by evaluation of the work
One short clause on who was affected or what would otherwise have happened
A longer title, since the title is where stakes are usually stated for readers
items.explanation: Stakes are a fact about consequences, stated briefly.

items.prompt: When should entries be made?
choices: Only at review time
Soon after the work
Once per year
items.explanation: Detail is freshest close to the event.

items.prompt: 'Made a huge impact' is:
choices: Still a self-assessment
A checkable fact
A before-and-after number
items.explanation: A superlative is a verdict however confident.

items.prompt: Which work does memory forget first?
choices: Flashy demos
Last week's headline event
Quiet, competent work
items.explanation: Quiet work lacks the drama memory keeps.

items.prompt: Should you invent a metric?
choices: Yes, because numbers look rigorous
No, state only checkable facts
Yes, whenever it rounds nicely
items.explanation: A fake number is worse than an honest fact.

items.prompt: What replaces a superlative?
choices: A fact
A bigger superlative
Silence
items.explanation: Each vague claim becomes something concrete.

items.prompt: Is routine mentoring worth logging?
choices: No, only dramatic incidents count
No, it is far too small
Yes, in the same factual style
items.explanation: Quiet work is exactly what gets lost.

items.prompt: 'No alert had caught it' is:
choices: A made-up statistic
An objective fact, even without a number
A subjective boast
items.explanation: Not every fact needs a figure.

items.prompt: Writing everything at review time repeats which problem?
choices: Reconstructing from memory
Having far too many notes
Being too accurate
items.explanation: It rebuilds the manager's weakness.

items.prompt: Someone logs only the loud wins. Six months later the log holds three launches and nothing else. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: The packet is balanced, since the biggest wins always represent the whole period
The packet shows spikes and misses the steady reliability and mentoring work
The packet is stronger, since a short list is easier for a committee to read
The packet is weaker only for the launches, since quiet work never matters
items.explanation: Quiet work is both what memory forgets and what shows consistent judgment.
items.reference:
Four ways a log goes wrong
📅 written only at review time: detail gone
🎈 vague superlatives: still a verdict
🎬 only dramatic wins: quiet work lost
🎲 invented numbers: worse than none
Why: each habit fixes one way memory or wording quietly erodes the record.
items.learnMore:
Fresh detail is the asset

The log's value is the detail captured while it is fresh. Writing late reproduces the manager's reconstruction problem.

Common mistake

Saving the log for the review. By then the specifics are the first thing to go.
items.reflection: What is the smallest note you could make this week that you would otherwise lose by the next review?

items.prompt: A work item has no metric at all. Which entry style fits the unit?
choices: State the checkable facts, such as no alert existing, and skip the number
Estimate a percentage that sounds plausible, so the entry looks complete to readers
Leave the item out, since entries without figures never help a promotion packet
Use a strong superlative, since confident wording can stand in for a missing number
items.explanation: A made-up figure damages trust; true facts without numbers are fine.

Delete the sentence, because reliability work cannot be written down

items.prompt: Draft A is:
choices: Overclaimed
Fully checkable
Under-described
items.explanation: It drops the facts and undersells the work.

items.prompt: Draft B is:
choices: A plain list of exact numbers
A verdict dressed as a report
A neutral and complete changelog
items.explanation: It claims readiness instead of stating facts.

items.prompt: Draft C is:
choices: Facts a stranger can judge
A short, polite apology
A formal request for a raise
items.explanation: It states what changed and lets the reader conclude.

items.prompt: Which draft says 'wasn't a big deal'?
choices: Draft B
Draft C
Draft A
items.explanation: That modest phrasing undersells the work.

items.prompt: Which draft says 'shows I'm ready'?
choices: Draft A
Draft B
Draft C
items.explanation: That is a verdict the writer cannot issue.

items.prompt: Who can use Draft C nearly unedited?
choices: The manager writing the packet
Nobody, because it is unusable
Only the engineer who wrote it
items.explanation: It already states facts a committee can evaluate.

items.prompt: Draft C avoids which phrase?
choices: 'Found by log correlation'
'Before any tickets arrived'
'Shows I'm ready'
items.explanation: It contains facts and no verdict.

items.prompt: A race condition is:
choices: A contest between teams
A timing bug from unlucky ordering
A kind of speed test
items.explanation: Two actions happen in a damaging order.

items.prompt: An engineer is told Draft B is 'honest, just confident.' Which response fits the unit?
choices: It is dishonest, since confident writing is always meant to deceive readers
It is ideal, since confidence is what persuades a promotion committee best
It is equal to Draft C, since both end up claiming that the work was good
It is not about honesty; it swaps facts for a verdict the reader cannot check
items.explanation: The failure is calibration, not truthfulness.
items.reference:
Three drafts, one event
🙈 A: under-described, no facts
📣 B: verdict replaces facts
✅ C: checkable facts, no verdict
Why: A and B fail in opposite directions; C is the only one a manager can reuse as written.
items.learnMore:
Neither anxiety is more honest

Draft A hides facts out of modesty. Draft B adds a verdict out of overcorrection. Both leave the reader with little to evaluate.

Common mistake

Treating confident wording as persuasive. Specific, checkable facts persuade more.
items.reflection: Which pull do you feel more, hiding the work or inflating it? What would the plain fact version say?

It names the writer's team, which is the factor committees weigh most
items.explanation: The evidence sits where the reader can inspect it.

items.reflection: Which pull do you feel more, hiding the work or inflating it? What would the plain fact version say?

items.prompt: Must objective framing use a number?
choices: Yes, always
Only for weekend work
No, only a checkable claim
items.explanation: Observable signs count as evidence.

items.prompt: Which is checkable?
choices: Helped a teammate grow a lot
The teammate fixed the next two bugs unaided
Was a great mentor
items.explanation: Two events can be looked up.

items.prompt: An observable sign is:
choices: Something that happened afterward and can be seen
A private feeling
A promise for next year
items.explanation: It is evidence others can verify.

items.prompt: Which could be an observable sign?
choices: A compliment you gave yourself
A longer job title
A decision another team adopted
items.explanation: Adoption by others is verifiable.

items.prompt: 'Fewer repeated blockers' is:
choices: A verdict
A checkable sign
An invented statistic
items.explanation: It can be compared before and after.

items.prompt: Can a design decision be written objectively?
choices: Yes, using adoption or citations
No, it has no incident count
Only if it was a bug fix
items.explanation: The claim only needs to be checkable.

items.prompt: The test for a claim is:
choices: Does it sound modest?
Is it long enough?
Could a reader check it?
items.explanation: Checkability, not numbers, is the requirement.

items.prompt: Why is this unit's example a case, not the whole territory?
choices: It covers every possible kind of work
Other kinds of work need their own signs
It only applies to Saturdays
items.explanation: Each kind of work has different checkable specifics.

items.prompt: A writer mentored a teammate and has no metric. Which entry best follows the unit?
choices: Helped a teammate grow into a much stronger engineer over several months
Invented a growth score of 8 out of 10 for the teammate's progress
Mentored well, as shown by how often the teammate said thank you
Paired for three sessions; the teammate then solved the next two similar bugs alone
items.explanation: It names events others can look up, with no invented number.
items.reference:
Checkable, not numeric
🔢 a number is one kind of evidence
👀 an observable sign is another
🔍 the test: could a reader verify it?
Why: objective framing needs a claim checkable against something real, not necessarily a figure.
items.learnMore:
Evidence without a metric

Mentoring, design decisions, and review work leave observable signs: events that happened afterward, which others can look up.

Common mistake

Concluding that work without a number cannot be written objectively.

items.prompt: Which design-decision claim is checkable?
choices: It was widely seen as a thoughtful and mature piece of design work
It was probably the reason things went smoothly for the whole group
Two other teams built on it without asking for any changes to it
It reflects strong judgment and a good sense of long-term trade-offs
items.explanation: Adoption without rework is an event; the rest are verdicts.

items.prompt: Someone says: 'If I have no metric, I should skip the log entry.' What is the best reply?
choices: Agree, since entries without a number carry no weight with any committee
Record the observable signs instead; the claim must be checkable, not numeric
Add an estimated percentage, so the entry matches the others in the log
Replace it with a verdict, since praise can stand in for missing figures
items.explanation: Absence of a metric is not absence of evidence.

items.prompt: If the audience were a hiring manager outside the company, what most likely needs adding to Draft C?
choices: Context an outsider lacks, such as what the system does and why silent data damage matters
A stronger verdict, because strangers need to be told how impressive it was
Less detail, because outsiders only read the headline of each entry
The same text, because every reader already shares the writer's context
items.explanation: The facts stay; the background an insider takes for granted must be supplied.
